newsitem.title: ITALY: Turkey says no territorial claims on Greek land.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says no territorial claims on Greek land.

text.p: Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Tuesday Ankara had no territorial claims on Greek land and appealed to the international community to help spur talks with Athens to end the "political nonsense".
"We have no territorial claims whatsoever at all," Ciller said on the eve of talks with five European colleagues expected to address the increasing tensions between the NATO allies.

"Whatever disputes we have should be solved on an individual basis with dialogue," Ciller said. "Turkey is large enough. We don't want anything that belongs to Greece at all. We only want what is ours as justified in international terms."

Greece and Turkey almost went to war last year over the sovereignty of a tiny outcrop of Aegean Sea islands and tensions have recently flared again over the divided island of Cyprus, which Turkey invaded in 1974 after a Greek-backed military coup.
"We only want what is ours as is justified in international terms," Ciller told a question-and-answer session at the Italian Institute of International Affairs, speaking in English.
Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis accused Turkey in a speech to socialist leaders in Rome last week of pursuing "a policy of aggression" in the Aegean against international law.
Greece has asked Turkey to engage in "a step by step approach" to solve their differences, including submitting rival territorial claims to the International Court of Justice.
Athens has said it would be ready to abide by any ruling from the Court of Justice but has slammed what it sees as a lack of will on Turkey's part so far.
Ciller said Greece and Turkey were neighbours with much in common. "It's the political nonsense, in quotation marks, that separates these people," she said.

Tensions between the two have escalated recently over plans by the Greek Cypriot government, the only internationally recognised power on the island, to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles in Cyprus.
Turkey, which has a self-declared Turkish Cypriot republic and 30,000 troops in the northern third of the island, responded with threats of military retaliation.

Ciller said Ankara "would never initiate a crisis" and said Turkey was the victim of wider efforts to exclude it from the European Union. Turkey has a customs union but feels its efforts to become a full member of the 15-nation bloc are being held up.
"What we would want you to do is to see this as not just a Turkish-Greek conflict on its own. It's not," she said.
"Greek moderates feel they should sit down and talk with us," she said. "We are ready...So the encouragement should be for dialogue as was the case in Bosnia and in the Middle East."
Wednesday's talks, with foreign ministers from France, Germany, Britain, Spain and Italy, are informal and no European Union decisions can be taken.
